My question: I know it's possible to grow an avocado tree from the pit. Do I just throw it in the ground, or what? I'm in a subtropical climate and they grow here... I just don't know the first step.

I love it! Avocados do grow from the pit, but you might want to look it up. It may be quicker to get some young trees or cuttings from a nursery. I have heard that avocados take about 15 years to produce fruit, so you might want to get on that now! Also make sure you don't need more than 1 tree for production, I know apples and peaches do.

I've done the avocado from a pit. I washed clean the oil residue and skewered the pit in three directions so that it can be suspended in the mouth of a container with the spot facing down. Then I kept it full of water at just halfway up or less on the pit.

After two weeks or so in a sunny window, the pit skin flakes off and the pit splits as it prepares to put down a root. Keep the water clean and topped up until the root descends and it puts up leaves, which could be a week later. It is not a fast process, possibly because it's not subtropical here.

The avocados would likely be much worse than the fruit the pit came from due to cross pollination so buy/graft a cutting of a cultivated variety if you really want good fruit.

Hi everyone! Just sharing this tip that I have found to work out very well when making various in-ground beds. Instead of purchasing weed barrier, you can use cardboard as a weed barrier. You can cut the cardboard to fit the shape of the bed, and add a few layers. The cardboard will prevent weeds from coming into your bed, and will also decompose in the ground (organic matter, anyone?). I have only used cardboard for one season (started last fall), but I've also read that once it has decomposed, there's no need to replace it because weeds will have given up after so many years. I've been using cardboard scraps from Christmas gifts or grocery shopping for my weed barrier, and nothing seems to get through it.
A cheap (or free) alternative to weed barrier
